summary: A 1975 description of the internal states of an NCP connection in the TENEX implementation, drawn as a finite state machine.

plainLanguage.summary: A connection moves through steps, like a phone call: dialing, ringing, talking, hanging up. This note lists those steps for one early system.

subtitle: The state machine controlling TENEX NCP connections.

tldr.problem: An NCP must manage network connections through many states: before connection, during data transfer, and during close-down. Bugs can occur when unexpected events happen in the wrong state.
tldr.mechanism: TENEX version 1.33 uses a finite state machine with 14 states (closed, listening, open, etc.), 14 event types (incoming RFC, close, timeout, etc.), and corresponding actions for each state-event pair.
tldr.outcome: The state machine ensures orderly connection setup and teardown and handles timeouts and errors gracefully. It is a clear model for other implementers.

today: RFC 689 documents the internal implementation of TENEX NCP as it existed in 1975. Modern network stacks use similar finite state machines to manage connection lifecycles.

sections.title: Connection States
sections.content: A network connection must pass through a series of states from creation to deletion. In TENEX NCP version 1.33, a connection begins in the CLOSED (CLZD) state. When a program requests a connection or receives a request from the network, the connection moves to intermediate states such as PENDING, LISTENING, or RFC SENT (waiting for acceptance). Once both sides have exchanged RFCs (Remote Function Calls), the connection enters the OPEN (OPND) state where data can flow. Finally, when closing, the connection passes through states like CLOSE WAIT (CLSW) before returning to FREE.
sections.plainLanguage: A connection has stages: waiting to start, trying to connect, reading to talk, talking, and saying goodbye. The state machine names them all.

sections.title: Events and Transitions
sections.content:
Each state can receive events such as an incoming RFC (RRFC), a close request from the local program (CLZR or CLZS), a close from the remote end (CLSR or CLSS), or a timeout (TIME). When an event occurs in a state, the FSM executes an action such as sending an RFC (ARFC), closing the connection (ACLS), or opening link tables (AOPL). Not all events are valid in all states. If an unexpected event occurs, the FSM generates an error action (AFNY, a "funny" or unexpected event).

Most states timeout after two minutes of inactivity (TIME event). In states where the program is listening for a connection, the timeout does not apply. In states where data is being transferred, a timeout triggers a resynchronization of allocation if the remote host supports that extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Different things can happen at each stage. Receiving a close request while open means something different than receiving one while listening. The machine knows what to do at each stage.

sections.title: Open and Closing Sequence
sections.content:
Once in the OPEN state, data can flow freely between the two sides. Both send and receive paths are active. If the local program closes a receive side, the connection moves to CLOSE WAIT 1 (CLW1) and a CLS (close) is sent to the remote end. If the local program closes a send side, the connection moves to DATA WAIT (DATW) and waits for the final RFNM (Request for Next Message) acknowledgment of the last data before sending CLS.

Closing can be complex because the local side may close while data is still in flight from the remote side. The FSM handles this by moving to intermediate states like RFN1 (awaiting the final RFNM) and RFN2 (final RFNM wait after an unexpected close). The connection is not fully freed until both sides have closed and all outstanding messages have been acknowledged.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone hangs up on a phone call, the other person hears silence. But if both people are talking, they have to finish their sentences and say goodbye properly. The state machine makes sure that happens.

sections.title: The Complete Picture
sections.content:
The TENEX FSM defines 14 states, 14 events, and 13 possible actions. Each state description lists which events are expected and what action and next state result. This clarity prevents many bugs: an event that is unexpected in a given state is explicitly marked as a "funny" event, and the system logs an error rather than silently doing something wrong.

The FSM is a working model of the NCP as it was implemented in TENEX and serves as a template for other implementations. It separates the concept of a host-level close (CLZF) from a protocol-level close (CLS), and it carefully manages the transition from active data transfer to connection cleanup.
sections.plainLanguage: The state machine is like a flowchart of all the paths a connection can take. It makes sure the computer and the network never get confused about what stage they are in.
